issues.item: Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies cluster is not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Excessive exercise and alcohol use can occur in PTSD, but in this profile they are hard to connect to the dominant threat-memory pattern centered on danger vigilance after a motor vehicle collision. With no trigger links active, these strategies should still fit the patient’s central formulation via memory/threat/appraisals, yet these two items feel relatively generic and not clearly tied to the reported intrusive reliving, vigilance, and environmental scanning.

Dehumanization is the main inconsistent appraisal. Feeling like an object is more characteristic of interpersonal trauma involving humiliation, coercion, or abuse than a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. It also sits awkwardly beside the rest of the profile, which is strongly organized around danger anticipation, distrust, and reliving of the crash. In contrast, shame on recall plus dehumanization suggests a different trauma meaning that is not otherwise represented in the memory, threat, or strategy items.

issues.item: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, intense shame on recall is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the rest of the content. The other memory items emphasize sensory reliving and replay, while no appraisal item directly explains shame about the event (e.g. self-blame, humiliation, permanent damage). This makes the shame item clinically hard to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is more characteristic of interpersonal trauma, coercion, or dehumanizing abuse than a motor vehicle collision. In this profile there are no companion items about bodily violation, humiliation, or identity damage that would make this appraisal cohere after an MVC.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies a generalized interpersonal mistrust. For an MVC profile dominated by danger scanning and reliving, that belief is possible but is not well anchored by the trauma type or by other selected items, which focus on environmental threat rather than betrayal or intentional human threat. This creates a cross-node mismatch in the formulation content.

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: This item is the main coherence problem. For a 24-year-old female survivor of a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the rest of the profile is tightly organized around fear-based PTSD: hypervigilant threat monitoring, danger-focused appraisals, and highly sensory reliving memory. 'Seeking Conflict' reflects an externalizing/drama-generating coping style that is not supported by the other selected items and does not fit the predominant cognitive formulation as well as the other strategies do. Alcohol use and checking surroundings plausibly connect to threat and memory, but picking arguments to distract herself pulls toward a different presentation and is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Alcohol Use: drink alcohol
issues.explanation: Alcohol use is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected content. The other items depict a tightly fear-based, hypervigilant motor-vehicle-collision presentation focused on environmental scanning, sleep vigilance, back-to-wall positioning, reliving, and danger-based appraisals. A solitary alcohol-use item without any parallel avoidance/numbing/interpersonal dysregulation content makes the coping pattern feel clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, generalized scanning for threat is coherent, but specifically 'noticing weapons' pulls toward assault/interpersonal violence content. Given that the rest of the profile is entirely accident-based and contains no interpersonal-threat, attack, or weapon-related memory/appraisal material, this item is difficult to reconcile with the otherwise coherent accident formulation.

vignette:
Nadia is a 24-year-old single Arab American woman who works long hours as a tailor in a small alterations shop, spending most of her day bent over hems and seams while customers come and go behind her. Six months before seeking treatment, she was driving home after closing when another car ran a red light and slammed into the driver’s side of her sedan. She remembers the impact as a violent sideways blast of metal and glass, the cabin suddenly folding inward, the sound so loud it seemed to erase thought. For a few seconds she was certain she would die there, trapped in the car and unable to predict what would hit next. In the aftermath, what stayed with her most was not only the crash itself but the sense that danger had appeared without warning, from an ordinary moment she had not seen coming.

Since then, Nadia has come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that a person has to stay especially careful because disaster can arrive at any second. She is more wary of other people too, feeling that people are not always what they seem and that safety depends on not relaxing around them. From that position, her habits have changed in ways that feel sensible to her. She avoids driving altogether and refuses rides unless absolutely necessary, arranging her life around walking, rideshares she can cancel at the last minute, and favors from relatives. In the shop, she chooses the chair that lets her keep her back to the wall and her eyes on the front door. She also rehearses disasters in her mind—what if a customer becomes aggressive, what if a car jumps the curb, what if she gets trapped somewhere again—because she feels she must think through the worst in order to be ready.

The memories themselves remain raw and immediate. When something reminds her of the collision, it does not feel like recalling a past event; it feels as though she is back in the driver’s seat at the instant of impact. She describes the scene replaying like a film she cannot stop, and each replay brings the same terror she felt that night. Those moments push her further into protective routines. If she hears tires screech outside the shop or catches sight of a dented fender on the street, she begins scanning exits, checking who is near her, and telling herself not to get into any vehicle unless there is no alternative. The more vividly the crash returns, the more convinced she becomes that she must stay on guard.

That sense of current threat is now threaded through her days and nights. Nadia constantly scans her surroundings for signs of danger, tracking footsteps, traffic noise, and sudden movements before she can focus on her sewing. She has difficulty falling asleep because she feels she needs to remain alert; lying in bed, she listens for sounds outside and imagines what she would do if something happened. In restaurants or waiting rooms she cannot settle unless her back is against a wall and she can see the whole room. Living this way keeps the collision close. Her body is already braced, her attention fixed on possible danger, and in that keyed-up state the crash returns more easily and more forcefully, as if her mind is always only a step away from the scene.

These habits that are meant to protect her have gradually tightened around her. By avoiding driving and mentally preparing for catastrophe, she has less contact with ordinary experiences that might feel safe, and she takes her continued vigilance as proof that her fears are justified. Each day organized around watching, checking, and preparing confirms her belief that the world is dangerous and that trusting others would be naïve. The constant scanning also leaves her jumpy and tired, which makes her feel even less able to let her guard down. At work, customers have noticed that she startles when the shop bell rings and that she positions herself to watch them closely; one coworker told her she seems far away even while pinning a hem. Nadia feels ashamed of that, but she also believes it would be reckless to behave otherwise.

Over the past several weeks, the cycle has become harder for her to contain. Her sleep has worsened, the replaying memories are more frequent, and getting through a day at the shop now requires so much vigilance that she goes home exhausted but still unable to rest. She finally sought help after turning down a promising tailoring job because it would have required a commute by car. What frightens her most is the thought that she may never feel safe again, that one ordinary moment can always split open into catastrophe, and that if she stops watching for it, she will be caught defenseless the next time it comes.
